steps.title: Import libraries and create DataFrame
steps.instructions: Create groupby.ipynb, import pandas and numpy, and build the 50-row employee dictionary data. Convert it into df with pd.DataFrame(data) and run df.head() (Shift+Enter).

targets.caption: Convert the synthetic employee dictionary into a Pandas DataFrame

hints: Start by importing pandas as pd and numpy as np in your first notebook cell.
Use np.random.choice and np.random.randint to generate 50 records in a dictionary named data.
Pass data to pd.DataFrame(data), assign it to df, and call df.head() in a new cell.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to run the import cell before creating the dictionary with np.random.
Generating arrays of mismatched lengths instead of 50 items per column.
steps.code: import pandas as pd; import numpy as np; data = {'Department': np.random.choice(['Sales', 'Engineering', 'HR', 'Marketing'], 50), 'Employee': [f'Employee_{i}' for i in range(1, 51)], 'Salary': np.random.randint(40000, 120000, size=50), 'Experience_Years': np.random.randint(1, 15, size=50)}; df = pd.DataFrame(data); df.head()

steps.title: Compute average salary by department
steps.instructions: Group df by Department, select the Salary column, and compute the mean into avg_salary. Inspect it with head(2), sort_values(), and reset_index(), running each cell.

targets.caption: Group by Department and compute the mean Salary

explanations.topic: Groupby single column returns a Series

hints: Call df.groupby() with the grouping column name first.
Select ["Salary"] after groupby("Department") and chain .mean().
Call avg_salary.reset_index() to convert the Series result back into a DataFrame.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to select the numeric column Salary before calling .mean(), which fails on string columns in Pandas 2.x.
Confusing a grouped Series index with a regular DataFrame column before calling reset_index().

steps.title: Group by multiple columns
steps.instructions: Pass a list of Department and Experience_Years to df.groupby() and calculate the mean Salary into grouped. Display the first 10 rows with grouped.head(10).

targets.caption: Group by multiple columns using a list of column names

explanations.topic: MultiIndex results from grouping multiple columns

hints: When grouping by more than one column, what container type does groupby() expect?
Pass ["Department", "Experience_Years"] as a Python list inside df.groupby().
Chain ["Salary"].mean() and inspect the output using grouped.head(10).
common_mistakes: Passing multiple column names as separate arguments like groupby("Department", "Experience_Years") instead of a list.
Omitting the underscore in Experience_Years.

steps.title: Compute multiple aggregations with agg
steps.instructions: Group df by Department and call .agg() with a dictionary mapping Salary to mean, max, min and Experience_Years to mean, count. Assign to agg_result and display it.

targets.caption: Apply multiple aggregation functions per column with .agg()

explanations.topic: Mapping columns to aggregation lists in .agg()

hints: Use the .agg() method directly on df.groupby("Department").
Pass a dictionary where keys are column names and values are lists of aggregation strings.
Use {"Salary": ["mean", "max", "min"], "Experience_Years": ["mean", "count"]}.
common_mistakes: Selecting a single column before .agg() when trying to aggregate multiple different columns.
Passing function names without quotes as undefined variables instead of string names.

steps.title: Apply custom lambda percentile
steps.instructions: In groupby.ipynb, group df by Department, select Salary, and .apply() a lambda calling np.percentile(x, 75). Store it in custom_agg and display it.

targets.caption: Compute the 75th percentile salary per department using apply and lambda

explanations.topic: Custom group functions with apply and lambda

hints: Which GroupBy method lets you run an arbitrary Python or NumPy function on each group?
Chain .apply() onto df.groupby("Department")["Salary"].
Pass lambda x: np.percentile(x, 75) inside .apply().
common_mistakes: Forgetting to pass 75 as the second argument to np.percentile(x, 75).
Calling .apply() on the whole DataFrame without selecting ["Salary"], causing percentile to fail on string columns.

steps.title: Chain groupby with sort_values
steps.instructions: In groupby.ipynb, chain .sort_values(ascending=True) onto df.groupby("Department")["Salary"].mean(). Store it in sorted_avg_salary and display it.

targets.caption: Chain sort_values directly after the groupby aggregation

explanations.topic: Chaining sort_values in the same groupby line

hints: You can chain Series methods directly after .mean().
Add .sort_values(ascending=True) right after .mean().
common_mistakes: Calling .sort_values() before .mean() on the GroupBy object instead of the aggregated Series.
Writing lowercase true instead of True in Python.

steps.title: Compare group size and count
steps.instructions: In groupby.ipynb, compute group_size with df.groupby("Department").size() and group_count with df.groupby("Department").count(). Display both to compare row counts vs. column-wise non-missing counts.

targets.caption: Compare .size() Series output against .count() DataFrame output

explanations.topic: Difference between size and count with missing values

hints: Use .size() on df.groupby("Department") to count total rows per group.
Use .count() on df.groupby("Department") to count non-NA values column-wise.
common_mistakes: Assuming .size() ignores NaN values when only .count() excludes missing values.
Forgetting parentheses on .size() or .count().
steps.code: group_size = df.groupby("Department").size(); group_size; group_count = df.groupby("Department").count(); group_count

steps.title: Build sales DataFrame and sum totals
steps.instructions: In groupby.ipynb, build a 100-row sales_data dict, convert it with pd.DataFrame into sales_df, then sum Revenue per Store and Quantity per Product using groupby() and .sum().

targets.caption: Compute total revenue per store using groupby and sum

hints: Generate the 100-period Date column using pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', periods=100, freq='D').
Group sales_df by "Store" for "Revenue" and by "Product" for "Quantity", calling .sum() on each.
common_mistakes: Using periods=50 instead of 100 in pd.date_range, which causes a length mismatch error.
Calling groupby on the old employee df instead of sales_df.
steps.code: sales_data = {'Store': np.random.choice(['Store_A', 'Store_B', 'Store_C'], 100), 'Product': np.random.choice(['Apples', 'Bananas', 'Cherries'], 100), 'Revenue': np.random.uniform(10.0, 500.0, 100).round(2), 'Quantity': np.random.randint(1, 50, 100), 'Date': pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', periods=100, freq='D')}; sales_df = pd.DataFrame(sales_data); total_revenue = sales_df.groupby("Store")["Revenue"].sum(); quantity_sold_per_product = sales_df.groupby("Product")["Quantity"].sum()

steps.title: Group sales by store and month
steps.instructions: In groupby.ipynb, group sales_df by "Store" and sales_df["Date"].dt.month, then compute the mean Revenue into avg_daily_revenue. Display avg_daily_revenue to inspect monthly averages per store.

targets.caption: Group directly by a datetime Series month component
Mean revenue per store and month

explanations.topic: Passing a derived Series like dt.month into groupby

hints: You can pass a Series directly inside the list passed to groupby().
Extract the month number from sales_df["Date"] using the .dt.month accessor.
Write sales_df.groupby(["Store", sales_df["Date"].dt.month])["Revenue"].mean().
common_mistakes: Putting "Date.dt.month" inside quotes as a string column name instead of evaluating sales_df["Date"].dt.month.
Writing .dt.month() with parentheses instead of accessing it as a property.

steps.title: Count high sales per store
steps.instructions: In groupby.ipynb, add a boolean column sales_df["High_Sale"] = sales_df["Revenue"] > 250, then group by Store and sum High_Sale into high_sales_count. Display high_sales_count.

targets.caption: Sum the boolean High_Sale column to count rows exceeding 250

explanations.topic: Using boolean columns and sum to count conditional rows

hints: Create a True/False column by comparing sales_df["Revenue"] > 250.
In Pandas, summing a boolean column counts how many True values exist.
Run sales_df.groupby("Store")["High_Sale"].sum().
common_mistakes: Using .count() instead of .sum() on the boolean High_Sale column, which counts both True and False rows.
Forgetting to assign the comparison back to sales_df["High_Sale"].
